title: Where the gods hid
hookLine: the gods hide from Death inside one syllable; why Hindus begin with om

cards: An old Upanishad tells this story. The gods were afraid of Death. So they hid inside the Vedas, the sacred hymns, and wrapped themselves in the hymns' meters like a cloak.
It didn't work. Death saw them there, the text says, the way you'd see a fish in water. So the gods rose up out of the hymns and slipped into one sound: om.
The deathless, the story calls it. The fearless. And having entered it, the gods became deathless.

teach.h: OM: THIS SYLLABLE IS ALL THIS.
teach.b: Why would a sound be a hiding place? This week's Upanishad, the Mandukya, answers in its first line. Om.
This syllable is all this. Everything that was, is and will be is om, and whatever is beyond time, that too is om. Not a symbol of all this.
In Sanskrit the word for syllable, akshara, also means the imperishable: what can't wear away. So the gods didn't hide in a word. They hid in the one thing that doesn't end.
That's one of Hinduism's biggest ideas: Brahman, the one reality under everything, can be met in a sound. It's why Hindus begin so many prayers with om.
Om namah shivaya. Om gam ganapataye namah. A priest's first breath at a puja; a grandparent's first word at dawn.

teach.h: A, U, M, AND THE SILENCE.
teach.b: Om is chanted as three sounds, a, u and m, flowing into each other, and then a silence after.
This week, the Mandukya maps those three sounds onto the three places you live every day: waking, dreaming and deep sleep. And the silence onto something it simply calls the fourth.
Today, om is printed on yoga mats and played on meditation apps as a nice, calm hum. Hindus mean more by it. Saying om, the tradition says, isn't making a relaxing noise.
It's saying the name of everything, and stepping, for one breath, into the sound the gods called deathless. Twelve verses. One syllable.

how: Om is chanted by Hindus at the start and end of prayers, recitations and many rituals; the Mandukya Upanishad, with Gaudapada's verse commentary (Karika), is a central text in Advaita Vedanta study.

games.q: you're one of the gods. Death can see you inside the hymns like a fish in water. where do you hide?
games.why: the gods entered om, the deathless, the fearless. the Mandukya says it's all this.

practice: If you're comfortable, chant om once, slowly, out loud or under your breath: let it rise out of silence, hum for a while, fade, and then stay in the silence after it.
If chanting isn't for you, listen to any sound in the room the same way: where it starts, how long it lasts, where it goes. Each time, rest in the quiet that follows.
